title: Stem Cell Impregnated Thread Reinforced Encapsulation Devices (THREDs) for Surgical Therapy of the Acute and Chronic Effects of Mesenteric Ischemia
text:
Mesenteric ischemia is a devastating intestinal problem that often requires surgical resection of necrotic
intestine. In this proposal, we aim to utilize an adult intestinal ischemia and reperfusion model as well as a
massive small bowel resection model to elucidate the underlying signaling mechanism that vertebral body
mesenchymal stem cells utilize to bring about functional recovery after injury. We will use these stem cells in
conjunction with an implantable, retrievable, nanoporous device as a novel delivery mechanism for the
treatment of mesenteric and intestinal ischemia.

title: Plasticity of auditory electrical synapses
text:
Electrical synapses, mediated by neuronal gap junctions, are widespread throughout the auditory pathway.
However, the functional roles and properties of electrical synapses in the auditory system remain poorly
understood. Changes in the strength of electrical synapses are known to dynamically reconfigure neuronal
circuits in various neural structures but in contrast to chemical synapses, little is known about the molecular
mechanisms that underlie changes in the strength of electrical synapses. The proposed research will lead to the
identification of novel molecular mechanisms involved in the regulation of electrical synapses that could
fundamentally change the way we understand the organization of circuits associated with auditory dysfunction,
thus contributing to the identification of novel therapeutic targets.

title: Small Animal Imaging Facility
text: PROJECT SUMMARY – Small Animal Imaging Facility The Small Animal Imaging Facility (SAIF) is the Abramson Cancer Center's (ACC) Shared Resource that provides state-of-the-art instrumentation, renowned faculty and technical support staff with the expertise necessary to apply a broad range of imaging modalities to small animal models. The SAIF was formed in 2006 as an amalgamation of existing cores and equipment and has grown steadily in both available resources and usage since its founding. Supported modalities in the SAIF include magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), computed tomography (CT), single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), ultrasound imaging, photoacoustic imaging and optical/bioluminescence imaging. Upgrades added since the last renewal include one new optical scanner (2016), one PET and two CT scanners (2017), complete console upgrade of one of the MRI scanners (2018) and an intraoperative fluorescence scanner (2019). The SAIF also provides housing for rats and mice, allowing longitudinal imaging studies to be performed over an extended period. Dr. James Delikatny was appointed as Director of the Optical/Bioluminescence Sub Core in 2010 and overall Director of SAIF in 2014 and continues in that capacity. Dr. Stephen Pickup has served as the Technical Director and Director of the MRI Sub Core since the founding of the SAIF. The resource is composed of four sub-cores, each focusing on a particular group of imaging modalities and led by faculty with extensive experience. The SAIF provides critical support to the ground- breaking research efforts of many ACC members. These high-impact investigations include: tracking of T-cells and tumor cells in animal models of CAR-T immunotherapy (Drs. June, Gill, Milone, Powell, Ruella), development of imaging methods for measuring tumor metabolism using hyperpolarized MRI (Dr. Gade) or PET with F-18 labeled glutamine (Drs. Zhou, Mankoff) and translation of targeted fluorescent dyes developed for optical imaging in animal models into the surgical realm for intraoperative detection of tumor margins and micrometastases (Drs. Singhal, Delikatny). ACC members accounted for 41 of 76 investigators (54%) using the Shared Resource during the most recent reporting period (07/01/18-06/30/19). SAIF supports the research of six ACC Programs (Breast Cancer, Cancer Therapeutics, Hematologic Malignancies, Immunobiology, Radiobiology and Imaging, and Tumor Biology). Non-invasive small animal imaging is critically important to cancer biology and cancer therapy and the SAIF continues to be the essential resource for advancing cutting- edge and rigorous research in this area.

title: Targeting the cancer glycocalyx
text:
All cells are coated with sugars, but cancer cells have altered sugar structures compared to their healthy
counterparts. This project focuses on understanding how cancer cell-surface sugars contribute to disease
progression, and on inventing new cancer therapies that target disease sugars.

title: CREATE-HS: A summer Research Experience for Emerging Scientists in High School
text:
There is a well-established need to develop cancer researchers and cancer care professionals that bring unique
and varied perspectives to the workforce, and a strong body of evidence indicates that engaging with students
at early phases of their education can positively impact their decision to pursue training in science, medicine,
and related fields. The Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center’s Cancer Research Experienced
for the Advancement and Training of Emerging Scientists in High School (CREATES-HS) aims to identify
promising high school students in the Columbus Metro area and provide them with a summer research and
career development experience that will illuminate a path towards a future in cancer research. Further,
participants will be provided with meaningful cancer survivor and community interactions to highlight the real
impact that their research can have in improving the lives of others.

title: Integrated Microscopy Facility
text: Microscopy is an essential technology for cancer investigators, providing imaging to test hypotheses about physiologic processes at the whole-animal, organ, cell, and now at near-molecular level. The Integrated Microscopy Facility (IMF) provides state-of-the-art imaging capabilities to University of Chicago Medicine Comprehensive Cancer Center (UCCCC) investigators and others. The major objective of the IMF is to provide imaging expertise and instrumentation to advance investigator-driven basic and translational cancer research and foster the research output of the investigators. The IMF offers all major light and confocal laser microscopy instrumentation (including wide-field instruments), in addition to super-resolution technologies (e.g., stimulated emission depletion or STED, localization, structured light). In the reporting period, IMF supported 79 unique UCCCC members (47% MMC, 9% CPC, 22% IC, 18% CET, 5% non-aligned members), with 179 peer-reviewed cancer-related federal grants and 103 peer-reviewed publications (48% in journals with impact factor ≥10). A key goal for the IMF is to keep operating costs within reach of all UCCCC laboratories; accordingly, IMF has made over $1.8M in equipment upgrades since 2018, all with institutional funds. Future efforts are aimed at maintaining the high-quality services offered. To meet evolving demands, IMF will continually evaluate rapidly evolving technologies to make state-of-the-art tools available for the specialized imaging needs of UCCCC investigators. Computational approaches (e.g., “deep learning” techniques) likewise are now enhancing data gathering and analyses. This Core will strive to align instrumentation capabilities with specialized imaging needs of the UCCCC Investigators.

title: Oxford Nanospore Technologies PromethlON 24 for long-read sequencing and direct nucleic acid modification detection
text:
This application requests an Oxford Nanopore Technologies PromethION 24, a long-read third generation
sequencing instrument. This instrument enables the sequencing of long stretches of DNA and RNA and can also
detect DNA and RNA modifications which allows researchers to more accurately assess complex stretches of
DNA and how RNA or DNA is changed in different disease, tissue, cell or developmental states. Data generated
using the PromethION 24 will overcome limitations of currently available short-read sequencers and will
significantly benefit NIH funded biomedical research at The Ohio State University.

title: Development of a Base Editing Gene Therapy to Treat Parkinson's Disease by Modulating LRRK2
text:
Parkinson’s disease currently lacks disease-modifying therapies, and existing treatments do not address the
underlying pathogenic mechanisms. This project will evaluate a gene therapy based on CRISPR base editing to
inactivate or precisely modulate the activity of LRRK2, a key genetic contributor to Parkinson’s disease. The
results will inform the development of durable therapeutic strategies for Parkinson’s disease as well as other
neurodegenerative disorders using genome editing technologies.

title: Dynamics of the cellular interactome
text:
Heat stress response is among the most fundamental stress adaptations and is critical for both prokaryotic and
eukaryotic cell survival. This project will develop and apply quantitative in vivo cross-linking technologies and
methods to gain greater insight on cellular interactome dynamics during stress response. These studies will
enable improved understanding of many human diseases including cardiovascular, neurodegenerative,
metabolic, aging and other mitochondrial diseases, as well as many types of cancers.

title: Functional Characterization of ABCA3 Genomic Variants
text:
Mutations in the ABCA3 gene are the most common genetic cause of childhood interstitial lung disease (chILD)
among infants and children. As medical treatments remain limited, affected patients may require lung
transplantation for survival. We will use human lung cell lines to determine how specific ABCA3 mutations cause
chILD and to discover FDA-approved medications to treat infants and children with chILD due to ABCA3
mutations.

title: Metastatic tracking of cancer subclones for collateral lethality prediction
text:
Metastatic breast cancer remains a leading cause of cancer deaths because, over time, tumors become
increasingly complex, heterogeneous, and resistant to treatment. This research will develop new computational
tools to track how tumors evolve and spread while identifying specific vulnerabilities that can be targeted with
existing drugs. The proposed study will utilize molecular techniques, tissue banks, organoid models, and
machine learning methods (including phylogeny algorithms and transformer models) to examine the
informational landscape of metastatic breast cancer that could ultimately lead to improved treatment regimens
and more precise treatment options.

title: Lipid-Based Interventions to Mitigate the Impact of Arsenic on Microglial Function and Neurobehavior
text:
Emerging evidence implicates arsenic in the etiology of anxious/depressive disorders and later life dementia,
effects likely mediated by microglial dysfunction. Given the tremendous gaps in treatment for these conditions,
molecules like lysophosphatidylcholine-docosahexaenoic acid (LPC-DHA) that cross the blood-brain barrier and
exert anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects in microglia may offer a new avenue for improving
neurobehavioral outcomes. Combining sophisticated in vivo and ex vivo research examining arsenic-induced
neurotoxicity and the protective mechanisms of LPC-DHA with individually tailored educational activities, this
training grant will equip the fellow for a career as a physician-scientist exploring and addressing the
environmental drivers of neurobehavioral disorders.

title: HSV alkaline nuclease as a target for antiviral therapy
text:
It is now estimated that over 1 in 5 adults worldwide has genital herpes, making this one of the most common
STDs worldwide. A majority of spread of both HSV1 and HSV2 is transmitted by asymptomatic individuals
unaware of their HSV-positive status. The goal of this grant is to develop antiviral agents that are active against
herpes simplex virus and can prevent partner transmission of this devastating virus.

title: Defining how UFMylation pathway inhibition enhances anti-tumor immunity
text:
Identifying novel therapeutic strategies to stimulate anti-tumor immunity has the potential to improve upon
existing cancer treatments. This work will use newly identified UBA5 chemical inhibitors and genetic loss of
function studies to investigate the UFMylation protein UBA5 as a therapeutic target to stimulate immunotherapy
response. We will quantify changes in the tumor microenvironment upon loss of UFMylation activity, determine
the efficacy of UBA5 inhibition to promote tumor response to adoptive cell therapies like TCR and CAR T cells,
and mechanistically identify how UBA5 inhibition promotes antigen processing and presentation by tumor cells.

title: I CAN DO Surgical ACP (Improving Completion, Accuracy, and Dissemination Of Surgical Advanced Care Planning) Trial
text:
Nearly 20 million older adults undergo major elective surgical procedures, yet very few receive
advance care planning (ACP). Patients and/or caregivers must make complex decisions, but many
are unprepared to articulate individual care goals and consequently, older adults may undergo
surgical and post-surgical treatments inconsistent with their values and goals. We will conduct a three
arm pragmatic randomized controlled trial, leveraging the electronic health record, in 3 geographically
distinct healthcare systems to determine the effectiveness of increasing support intensity with
improving ACP completion rates and increasing patient engagement with ACP (measured by survey).

title: Phenotypic and adaptive consequences of chromosomal rearrangements
text:
A more complete understanding of the genetic basis of trait variation and biological
adaptation remains a major goal in biology with implications for human health, including enhancing
early disease detection, precision medicine, and personalized risk assessment. Mounting evidence suggests
that large chromosomal rearrangements, such as deletions, duplications, inversions and translocations of
chromosomal segments, have a disproportionate eects on traits and possibly on human diseases. This
project will provide foundational knowledge about the possible impacts of chromosomal rearrangements
by analyzing their eects and evolution in three insect systems.

title: Elucidating stromal regulation of hematopoiesis through syndecan-2
text:
The stromal bone marrow microenvironment supports hematopoiesis through direct and indirect mechanisms to
maintain homeostasis and regenerate the hematopoietic system upon stress. Proteoglycans are abundantly
expressed by bone marrow stromal cells, yet little is known about how they influence hematopoiesis. In this
proposal, we will study the role of the heparan sulfate proteoglycan, syndecan-2, expressed by the stroma in
hematopoietic homeostasis and hematologic regeneration from stress.

title: Characterizing PrEP Need and Use in Eswatini: Individual and Programmatic Insights Through Data Triangulation and Novel Epidemiological Methods
text:
While Eswatini has almost met UNAIDS’ 95-95-95 goals for epidemic control, HIV incidence is declining at a
glacial pace, pointing to the need for comprehensive HIV prevention programs. Scale-up of HIV pre-exposure
prophylaxis (PrEP) began in 2018, and nearly 100,000 individuals have initiated PrEP in Eswatini since. The
proposed study will develop better methods to determine who could most benefit from PrEP (i.e., PrEP need)
in Eswatini, and whether that need is being met at programmatic and individual levels, to inform future HIV
prevention programs and continued PrEP scale-up.

title: Using genomic instability and hypoxia as predictors of placental dysfunction
text:
Preeclampsia is a leading cause of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality in the United States. The
proposed research investigates the role of genomic instability and hypoxia in the pathogenesis of preeclampsia.
Findings from this research are relevant to public health because they can support the development of
biomarkers that enable earlier detection, and thus treatment, of preeclampsia.
